name: Machiguenga
confidence_why: Snell's 1974 phonology, the only first-hand description, shows stress is contrastive (minimal pairs such as paníro 'your niece' and pániro 'one') and falls most often on the penult or antepenult, her 1998 and 2011 dictionaries and the Chineri et al. 2020 teaching grammar agree on the penult/antepenult alternation, and the only dissent, family-wide remarks in Aikhenvald 1999 and Chen 2019 (quoting Mihas 2017) that Kampa stress is not contrastive, rests on no Matsigenka data.

catalog_quote: 1.2.3. El Acento. El acento principal aparece con más frecuencia en la sílaba penúltima o antepenúltima del grupo intensivo. Cae en la última, sólo en el vocativo enfático, como en /iná/ '¡mamá!'. En esta posición está acompañado de una prolongación notable y de un cambio y disminución del tono. Muchas veces, también, la sílaba que precede a la antepenúltima, es la que recibe el acento principal cuando está formada por el primer miembro de una combinación de vocales. Por otro lado, existen pocas palabras con acento en la sílaba indicada: /pishimáatakye/ 'estás pescando con flecha'. [p.9, sec. 1.1.3] El acento. La actualización de un acento fonémico se comprueba por varios pares de palabras. Ej.: /paníro/ 'su sobrina (de usted)' y /pániro/ 'uno'; /samáni/ 'majás' y /sámani/ 'lejos'; /ikyianakyéro/ 'él está entrando' y /ikyianákyero/ 'él la está llevando en sus espaldas'. También aparecen acentos secundarios, los cuales, en nuestro análisis, hasta el presente, no se consideran según la colocación del acento principal. [p.5, sec. 1] Hay 17 consonantes en el machiguenga ...; cinco vocales /i,e,a,o,u/; y un fonema de acento /´/.

new_statements.translation: 1.2.3. Stress. Primary stress appears most frequently on the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable of the stress group. It falls on the final syllable only in the emphatic vocative, as in /iná/ 'mother!'. [...] Often, too, the syllable preceding the antepenult is the one that receives primary stress when it consists of the first member of a vowel sequence. [p.9, 1.1.3:] Stress. The existence of a phonemic stress is demonstrated by several word pairs, e.g. /paníro/ 'your niece' vs /pániro/ 'one'; /samáni/ 'paca' vs /sámani/ 'far'; /ikyianakyéro/ 'he is entering' vs /ikyianákyero/ 'he is carrying her on his back'.

Muchas veces, tambien, la silaba que precede a la antepenultima, es la que recibe el acento…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Snell treats stress as phonemic (a 'fonema de acento', with minimal pairs) but confined to a right-edge window: primary stress falls on the penult or antepenult of the stress group ('grupo intensivo'), never on the final syllable except in emphatic vocatives, and sometimes on the pre-antepenult when that syllable is the first vowel of a vowel sequence. Her later dictionaries (1998/2008 p.14; 2011 p.18) operationalise this as: penultimate stress is the unmarked default and antepenultimate stress is lexically marked with a written accent on headwords (pánkotsi vs tinti, punatagantsi). A native-speaker pedagogical grammar (Chineri et al. 2020 pp.224-226) adds that antepenult stress is very frequent and partly conditioned by vowel quality (weak penult e/i with strong antepenult a/o/u) and morphology (imperatives, -rika/-mera/-rira, many -empa reflexives), suggesting a sonority-sensitive system like closely related Nanti; no formal metrical analysis of Matsigenka itself was found.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Snell 1978 p.9: 'También aparecen acentos secundarios, los cuales, en nuestro análisis, hasta el presente, no se consideran según la colocación del acento principal' — secondary stresses exist but were left unanalysed (note 8 p.33 calls for further study of stress definition/distribution and its relation to rhythm groups).
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress only in emphatic vocative (iná), with lengthening and pitch change; pre-antepenult stress when it is V1 of a vowel cluster; a few words like pishimáatakye; under agitation/emphasis stress shifts antepenult->penult, sometimes with vowel doubling (néro ~ neéro/nehéro; poreatsíri ~ poreátsiri); note 9: primary stress never on /i/ as second member of a vowel cluster nor on the second of two identical vowels (except where root-initial /h/ is dropped: noíme ~ nohíme), /e/ of /ae/ never stressed; stressed vowels often lengthened, high pitch on the stressed syllable in isolation; Snell 2011: stress unpredictable in onomatopoeic words and variable in descriptive particles; Snell 2011 glosses the contrast as 'acento (o acento tonal)'.
new_statements.domain_note: Snell's domain is the 'grupo intensivo' (stress group of 2-20 syllables bounded by potential pause, exactly one primary stress) rather than the grammatical word; dictionary citation forms follow the penult-default/antepenult-marked convention. Data from Urubamba-area Matsigenka (materials gathered from 1952 on; dictionary distinguishes Alto vs Bajo Urubamba).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Urubamba-area Machiguenga/Matsigenka = mach1267 (Snell's informants Alto/Bajo Urubamba; Snell 1978 notes Solís 1973 described a different dialect). Nanti (nant1250), analysed by Crowhurst & Michael 2005 / Michael 2008, is a separate Glottolog language and was used only as comparative context.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is phonemic (minimal pairs). One main stress per 'grupo intensivo' (2-20 syllables), most often on the penult or antepenult; it can fall on the pre-antepenult when that syllable is the first member of a vowel cluster; final stress only in the emphatic vocative. Stressed vowels are often lengthened and carry high pitch in isolation. Under agitation/emphasis the stress may shift from antepenult to penult (/néro/ ~ /neéro/), and forms like /poreatsíri ~ poreátsiri/ fluctuate.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 9: 'También aparecen acentos secundarios, los cuales, en nuestro análisis, hasta el presente, no se consideran según la colocación del acento principal. Se necesita un estudio más detallado antes de poder presentar un análisis adecuado de los acentos.' (secondary stresses exist but are left unanalysed; note 8 p. 33 repeats that the definition and distribution of the stresses await further research)
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress only in the emphatic vocative (/iná/), with lengthening and pitch fall; stress moves antepenult > penult in agitated speech; note 9 p. 33: the main stress never falls on /i/ as second member of a vowel cluster nor on the second of two identical vowels (except where a root-initial /h/ is dropped: /nohíme/ [noíme ~ nohíme]), and /e/ as second vowel of /ae/ never takes the main stress.

Snell 2008 [1998] p. 13 takes the Urubamba-zone dialect as the standard for headwords and lists Madre de Dios forms as variants. Chen 2019 is about the Kampa family (Nomatsigenga, Ashéninka, Pajonal, Asháninka, Kakinte, Matsigenka); its Matsigenka data are harvested from Snell 2011 and its stress remark is family-wide, not Matsigenka-specific.

new_statements.quote: El uso del acento. Por lo general no se usa un acento escrito para indicar las sílabas acentuadas en el machiguenga. Sin embargo, para ayudar al lector a distinguir algunas palabras que se diferencian solamente por el acento y para mayor conveniencia del usuario no machiguengahablante, se escriben los acentos que caen en las antepenúltimas sílabas. [...] pánkotsi {ivanko}... casa; kiráari... rojo(a); arákintsi {iáraki}... efectos personales... No se escriben en las siguientes palabras cuyos acentos caen en la penúltima sílaba: punatagantsi... pagar; mantsigarintsi {imantsigane}... enfermedad; tinti... papaya
new_statements.translation: The use of the accent. In general no written accent is used to indicate the stressed syllables in Machiguenga. However, to help the reader distinguish some words that differ only by stress, and for the greater convenience of the non-Machiguenga-speaking user, the accents that fall on antepenultimate syllables are written. [...] pánkotsi {ivanko}... house; kiráari... red; arákintsi {iáraki}... personal effects... They are not written in the following words, whose stress falls on the penultimate syllable: punatagantsi... to pay; mantsigarintsi {imantsigane}... illness; tinti... papaya

readall_conflicts: One disagreement. Chen 2019 (p. 2), quoting Mihas 2017 on the Kampa subgroup as a whole, states that stress is not contrastive in Kampa varieties (nouns penultimate, verbs iambic feet with main stress on the final foot). Both Snell works say the opposite for Machiguenga specifically: Snell 1974 p. 9 demonstrates a phonemic stress with minimal pairs (paníro/pániro, samáni/sámani, ikyianakyéro/ikyianákyero) and Snell 2008 [1998] p. 13 writes accents precisely to separate 'palabras que se diferencian solamente por el acento'. Chen's sentence is a secondhand family-level generalisation with no Matsigenka stress data (his own data are unmarked for stress), so the primary descriptive sources prevail; the catalog's 'lexical (unpredictable)' reading stands, with the refinement that stress is confined almost entirely to the penult/antepenult window (penult the orthographic default, antepenult marked), pre-antepenult only on the first member of a vowel cluster, final only in the emphatic vocative. Snell 1974 herself flags that secondary stresses and the distribution of the stresses need further study (p. 9, note 8 p. 33).

sources.note: 'Alfabeto y pronunciación', p.18 'El uso del acento': orthographic accent normally not. to distinguish words differing only in stress ('acento (o acento tonal)') accents falling on antepenultimate syllables are written on headwords; 'Si no se escribe, el acento cae en la penúltima sílaba'; prosodic stress varies in many words; stress unpredictable in onomatopoeic words (examples pánkotsi, tinti, punatagantsi). Apuntes gramaticales 7.1 p.875: descriptive particles vary in stress/length/intonation by context. Refers to Snell 1974 and Solís 1973 for phonology.

sources.citation: Chineri Pinedo, Eusebio; Misael José Prialé Arias; Bruno Abras Turco; Lizbeth Mambiro Vicente; Gerardo Antón Zerdin. 2020. Guía teórica del idioma matsigenka / Giatakotirori aniane. Atalaya: Universidad Católica Sedes Sapientiae – Nopoki. 326 pp. (archive.org item guia-teorica-matsigenka-2020)
sources.note: Pedagogical (native-speaker authors), pp.224-226 'El acento en el idioma matsigenka' (fn. cites Aza 1923 pp.61-62): no tilde used; no final-stressed words or monosyllables except onomatopoeia; antepenult stress very frequent — when the penult vowel is weak (e,i) and the antepenult strong (a,o,u) (impókiro, mániro, magátiro), in imperatives (kánteri, névite), verb forms with pronominal affixes (nonkamánteri, ipákena), words in -rika/-mera/-rira (ogatsantsárika), many reflexives in -empa (mánempa, kishítempa); some -empa reflexives are penult-stressed (sekatémpa, kaatémpa, kaentémpa).

sources.note: p.14 'El uso del acento': same convention as 2011 — accents written only when on the antepenult (pánkotsi, kíraari, árakintsi); not written on words whose stress falls on the penult (punatagantsi, mantsigarintsi, tinti).
